objective: Make terminal recovery predictable and keep one canonical daemon in control
requirements: A terminal explicitly killed through TermFleet does not return automatically after restart
An untouched terminal returns after daemon failure or machine restart
A saved backup is inactive until the operator explicitly restores it
Only the canonical per-user daemon owns PTYs and recovery decisions
The installed dock-launched runtime proves the behavior
knownFailures: Explicitly killed terminals return as recovered terminals
A launcher, embedded fallback, or replacement daemon races the canonical daemon
A backup is mistaken for an automatically restorable session
A restart silently restores a terminal without explaining why
outOfScope: Changing terminal rendering or scrollback interaction
Changing provider conversation semantics beyond lifecycle ownership

successCriteria: Focused lifecycle and daemon ownership tests pass
Restart and close verification pass against the installed runtime
The installed release identity remains verified
The trusted verification artifact is fresh and independently sealed
failureSignals: An intentional kill is eligible for automatic restore
More than one process can own the canonical PTY socket
A backup is restored without an explicit restore action
The installed runtime cannot be identified or verified

sure.rootCause: Recovery eligibility is split between workspace tombstones, persisted PTY files, launcher helpers, and daemon fallback paths instead of one durable lifecycle decision owned by the canonical daemon.
sure.research: The existing PTY kill, persisted-session, hydration, daemon ownership, launcher, and close/restart paths were inspected and the independent regression surface is identified.
sure.fix: Make the canonical daemon record lifecycle disposition before killing, keep backups separate from restore candidates, and fail closed whenever daemon ownership is ambiguous.
sure.sideEffects: Untouched terminals retain crash/restart recovery; explicit kills stop returning; launcher and UI reconciliation become consumers of daemon state rather than competing controllers.
